library(tidyverse)
library(data.table)

Using PLINK

PLINK is a software to work with genomic data. It allows you to filter individuals, extract SNPs, and run basic statistics. Download PLINK and access the documentation here: https://www.cog-genomics.org/plink/

PLINK File Types

The main PLINK file types are: .bed, .bam, and .fam. You need each of these files in the same directory for most PLINK commands to work; they are generally not stand alone files.

When doing some work in R (such as RDA or random forest modelling) you can combine these files into a single human readable one, usually a .raw.

Let’s start by looking at these files.

The dataset

These are a few Atlantic Salmon populations in Newfoundland, which contain 220,000 SNPs that have been identified to be highly divergent between wild and aquaculture Atlantic salmon. For this tutorial, I have extracted a subset of samples to keep file sizes small. Note that the metadata has columns named “FID” (family ID) and “IID” (individual ID). These are used in PLINK.

Metadata <- fread("sampleSalmonMetadata.csv")
rmarkdown::paged_table(Metadata)

Mapping the data

library(leaflet)
leaflet(Metadata) %>% 
  addTiles() %>% 
  addMarkers(~Lon, ~Lat, popup = ~Rivername)

PLINK Files

First, the .fam file

This file contains no genotype data, just the list of individuals (FID and IID)

famFile <- fread("sampleSalmonDataset.fam")
rmarkdown::paged_table(famFile)

Next, the .bed file

This is not easily readable in R, open in a text editor.

The .bim file

This contains the chromosome, SNP ID, position, and nucleotides.

bimFile <- fread("sampleSalmonDataset.bim")
rmarkdown::paged_table(bimFile)

Using PLINK

PLINK runs in the command line, or can be called from R studio using system(). It uses “flags” (parameters and commands) denoted with two dashes (–). Some flags are always used for fish data, such as –allow-extra-chr. This is because PLINK’s default chromosome number is 23 and will throw an error if it gets more. Here is an example of the syntax of a PLINK command to filter for a single chromosome:

plink ##call PLINK
  --bfile sampleSalmonDataset ##Need to specify which dataset to use (.bim/.bed/.fam)
  --allow-extra-chr ##Always need this for non-human data
  --chr NC_059455.1 ## Keep only this chromosome 
  --make-bed ##Creates a new file with specified flags. Without this, no output would be created
  --out OneChrom ##Names the outfile bed/bim/fam

Running it using system() in R:

system("/opt/miniconda3/bin/plink --bfile sampleSalmonDataset --allow-extra-chr --chr NC_059455.1 --make-bed --out OneChr")

Often PLINK commands need other files, usually as a .tsv. For example, if we wanted to compare per-locus FST between two rivers, first we would want to make a new file (bed/bim/fam set) with just those two rivers. To do this, we will use the PLINK –keep flag. This requires a .tsv with just FID and IID of samples you want to keep. When we do FST later, we will need a third column with group/ cluster. We will make that column now to make it easier later, and PLINK can ignore it for the first step.

SheepscotCodroyID <- Metadata %>% 
  filter(FID == "SHP" | FID == "COD") %>% 
  select(FID, IID, Rivername)

#Make sure column and row names are turned off for the TSV
 write.table(SheepscotCodroyID, "SheepscotCodroyID.tsv", col.names = T, row.names = F, sep = "\t", quote = F)

The PLINK command will be similar to the one above, but replace the –chr flag with “keep”:

plink ##call PLINK
  --bfile sampleSalmonDataset ##Need to specify which dataset to use (.bim/.bed/.fam)
  --allow-extra-chr ##Always need this for non-human data
  --keep SheepscotCodroyID.tsv ## Keep only IIDs in this .tsv
  --make-bed ##Creates a new file with specified flags. Without this, no output would be created
  --out SheepscotCodroy ##Names the outfile bed/bim/fam

Running it using system() in R:

system("/opt/miniconda3/bin/plink --bfile sampleSalmonDataset --allow-extra-chr --keep SheepscotCodroyID.tsv --make-bed --out SheepscotCodroy")

Now to calculate FST, we use the dataset created above, with the –fst flag:

plink ##call PLINK
  --bfile SheepscotCodroy ##Dataset created above
  --allow-extra-chr ##Always need thSheepscotCodroyis for non-human data
  --maf 0.01 #generally best practice to set a minor allele frequency filter, but not strictly necessary 
  --fst 
  --within SheepscotCodroyID.tsv ##Groups to calculate FST between are in the third column of this tsv
## note make-bed is not needed
  --out ShpCod

Running it using system() in R:

system("/opt/miniconda3/bin/plink --bfile SheepscotCodroy --maf 0.01 --allow-extra-chr --fst --within SheepscotCodroyID.tsv  --out ShpCod")

PLINK makes many files (a large part of genomics is just file management.) These can often be read back into R (or excel, etc.) for further interpretation and analysis. For the FST analysis above, it created a file called ShpCod.fst. We can look at this:

fst <- fread("ShpCod.fst")
rmarkdown::paged_table(fst)

These commands to filter and calculate FST could have been done in the same PLINK command, like this:

plink \
  --bfile sampleSalmonDataset \
  --keep SheepscotCodroyID.tsv \
  --allow-extra-chr \
  --maf 0.01 \
  --fst \
  --within SheepscotCodroyID.tsv \
  --out ShpCod

The FST values can then be processed and plotted in R:

Bedtools

Bedtools can be used to detect overlaps in two genomic datasets (among other things): https://bedtools.readthedocs.io/en/latest/ To check if the outlier SNPs for any given metric are in genes, you need a file with all genes and their positions. Then use the bedtools intersect command.

First, we need determine which SNPs are FST outliers. I’ll arbitrarily use the top 1% of highest FST SNPs.

fstOutlier <- fst %>% 
  arrange(desc(FST)) %>% 
  filter(row_number() < nrow(fst) * 0.01)

rmarkdown::paged_table(fstOutlier)

For bedtools, we need to write a .bed file. This file needs to have the columns as: Chromosome, BP Start, BP End, SNP ID Since we are not looking at ranges of SNPs, BP start and BP end will just both be POS (position). If you were interested in looking at a range around the SNP, this can be done by subtracting from POSStart and adding to POSEnd. Column names don’t matter because they will not be written anyway.

fstBedPrep <- fstOutlier %>% 
  mutate(POSStart = POS) %>% 
  mutate(POSEnd = POS) %>% 
  select(c(CHR, POSStart, POSEnd, SNP)) %>% 
  distinct() #best practive to avoid duplicates


write.table(fstBedPrep,
  "HighFST_SHP_COD.bed", 
  col.names = F, 
  row.names = F, 
  sep = "\t", 
  quote = F)

Running bedtools

Bedtools runs like PLINK using flags. the -b file is our file, and the -a file is the file to compare it to. The -wb flag says to write both overlaps as an output, named “highFSTgenesSHP_COD” First, make sure that your file with genes and positions is in the same directory.

system("bedtools intersect -b HighFST_SHP_COD.bed -a Ssal3_1.genes.unique.bed -wb >  highFSTgenesSHP_COD.tsv")

Now we can read back in the genes file: (Genes are in V4)

hiFSTgenes <- fread("highFSTgenesSHP_COD.tsv")
rmarkdown::paged_table(hiFSTgenes)

The genes can then be pasted in ShinyGO: https://bioinformatics.sdstate.edu/go/ for gene pathways!

Was that very high FST SNP on chr 1 in a gene?

Easy to check. Our “b” dataset is written after the a dataset in the datafrmae. Let’s get the SNP ID, Chromosome, and Position, then re-merge with the FST dataset.

cleanedFST <- hiFSTgenes %>% 
  rename("Gene" = "V4",
         "CHR" = "V5",
         "POS" = "V6",
         "SNP" = "V8") %>% 
  select(c(CHR, POS, SNP, Gene)) %>% 
  merge(fstOutlier) %>% 
  arrange(desc(FST)) 

rmarkdown::paged_table(cleanedFST)

Interestingly, it wasn’t! But lots of high FST SNPs are.
